# When to animate (house standards, version 4)

<!-- generated by tools/build_data.py from synthesis/; edit the source, not this file -->

The gate before any motion: how often people see it and what purpose it serves decide whether it animates at all, and how much.

Rules from non-negotiable sources. **must**: never break it without the person's explicit override. **should**: the default; say so when you depart from it. How to change one: `../standards.md`.

### STD-when-to-animate-01: Decide whether to animate first
**must**. Before choosing any tool, easing or duration, decide whether the element should animate at all (how often it is seen) and name its purpose; if either check fails, ship no animation.
- Values: decision-order: frequency, then purpose; only then tool, properties, easing and duration
- Why: Steps 1 (should this animate at all) and 2 (what is the purpose) gate everything: don't reach for a curve before you know whether it animates. Done wrong, animation makes an interface feel unpredictable, slow and annoying and can cost user trust.
- Sources: S-L19-012, S-L19-018, S-L19-016, S-L19-023, S-L19-024

### STD-when-to-animate-03: Name a valid purpose for every animation
**must**. Name each animation's purpose as feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation or delight (delight only at the rare/first-time tier); if none fits, including 'it looks cool', do not animate.
- Values: valid-purposes: feedback, spatial consistency, state indication, preventing a jarring change, explanation, delight (rare/first-time only)
- Why: Every animation must answer 'why does this animate?'. Motion should serve a function (orient, give feedback, show relationships), not just decorate, and 'it looks cool' on a frequently seen element is a reason to stop.
- Sources: S-L19-012, S-L19-018, S-L19-016, S-L19-023, S-L19-024, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033, S-L19-019

### STD-when-to-animate-04: Scale motion down as frequency rises
**must**. Estimate how often a person will see each animation (100+ times a day, tens of times a day, occasionally, or rarely / first time) and make it shorter and subtler the more often it is seen, down to no animation.
- Values: tiers: 100+ times/day; tens of times/day; occasional; rare / first-time
- Why: How often users will see an animation is a key factor in deciding whether to animate: the more often it is seen, the shorter and subtler it should be, because repeated animation stops being a pleasant surprise, becomes irritating and slows people down.
- Sources: S-L19-012, S-L19-019, S-L19-032, S-L19-027, S-L19-024

### STD-when-to-animate-05: No motion on 100+ times-a-day actions
**must**. Give no animation to anything people trigger or see 100+ times a day, such as a launcher or command palette opening and closing, keyboard shortcuts and core navigation (on iOS and Android also tab switches, keyboard open/close, scrolling and settings toggles: platform default or nothing).
- Values: frequency: 100+ times/day
- Why: Raycast is opened hundreds of times a day and has no open or close animation, which is the optimal experience; animating it every time would be very annoying.
- `engine.py review` checks it: A command palette opens 100+ times a day: remove the open/close transition or animation (open it instantly).
- Sources: S-L19-012, S-L19-018, S-L19-016, S-L19-023, S-L19-024, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033, S-L19-031, S-L19-030

### STD-when-to-animate-06: Never animate keyboard-initiated actions
**must**. Never animate an action started from the keyboard, including shortcuts, command-palette toggles, focus jumps and moving a list highlight with the arrow keys; the change happens instantly.
- Why: Keyboard actions may be repeated hundreds of times a day, and animation makes them feel slow, delayed and disconnected from the user's actions; an animated highlight lags behind the keys pressed. This is a disqualifier, not a judgment call.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Command-menu items are moved through with the arrow keys: remove the item transition so the highlight moves instantly.
- Sources: S-L19-012, S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-024, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033

### STD-when-to-animate-07: Remove or shrink motion seen tens-of-times daily
**must**. For things people see tens of times a day (hover effects, list navigation, frequent toggles, press feedback, row selection), remove the animation, or the hover interaction itself, or reduce it to near-imperceptible, fast and subtle motion; in React Native keep it under 150ms. List navigation with the arrow keys is keyboard-initiated and gets no animation.
- Values: frequency: tens of times/day; react-native-ceiling: under 150ms; native-press-ceiling: 120ms and a 3% scale
- Why: Seen tens, maybe even hundreds of times a day, animations and hover interactions stop delighting, quickly become annoying and make the interface feel slower; a hover effect used multiple times a day likely benefits most from no animation at all.
- Sources: S-L19-003, S-L19-012, S-L19-018, S-L19-016, S-L19-023, S-L19-024, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033, S-L19-015

### STD-when-to-animate-08: Standard motion for occasional surfaces
**should**. Give surfaces people meet occasionally (modals, drawers, sheets, toasts, settings; onboarding steps in the Expo table) standard animation, not delight motion.
- Values: frequency: occasional
- Why: The frequency tables give occasional UI standard animation and keep the delight budget for the rare/first-time tier. The Expo table lists onboarding steps as occasional, while the web tables put onboarding in the rare tier.
- Sources: S-L19-018, S-L19-016, S-L19-023, S-L19-024, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033

### STD-when-to-animate-09: Spend delight only on rare moments
**must**. Spend delight motion (motion whose purpose is delight, such as a decorative bounce, a generous stagger or a longer beat) only on rare or first-time, high-emotion moments such as onboarding and first run, empty states, success or completion, feedback forms and celebration, and never on components people use multiple times a day.
- Values: frequency: rare / first-time
- Why: Seen rarely, delight is a pleasant surprise that makes the experience memorable; used multiple times a day the component quickly becomes irritating, the initial delight fades and the animation slows users down. Rare moments rendered flat are where missing delight is worth adding.
- Sources: S-L19-012, S-L19-018, S-L19-016, S-L19-023, S-L19-024, S-L19-025, S-L19-032, S-L19-033

### STD-when-to-animate-10: Explanatory motion only in marketing, onboarding
**must**. Use explanation motion (animation that demonstrates how a feature works) only on marketing and onboarding surfaces.
- Why: Explanation is a valid purpose only on marketing and onboarding surfaces; Linear used an animation instead of a static asset so visitors understand what Product Intelligence does straight in the initial viewport.
- Sources: S-L19-018, S-L19-024, S-L19-012

### STD-when-to-animate-11: Keep decoration off functional data
**must**. Do not move data people are reading or acting on for style: keep decorative motion such as mouse-tracking, spring-driven interactive graphs and animated line drawing off functional, information-dense UI and charts, and use it only on marketing pages and illustrations.
- Why: Decoration on functional, information-dense UI hinders; on a functional graph in a banking app no animation is better, and a useSpring interactive graph is meant for illustrations, not functional graphs like stock charts.
- Sources: S-L19-018, S-L19-023, S-L19-024, S-L19-001, S-L19-033

### STD-when-to-animate-13: No entrance stagger on all-day lists
**must**. Do not give a stagger or entrance animation to a list people scroll past or use all day: it should already be there. Keep staggered entrances for lists and grids seen occasionally and for content the person asked for and is waiting on.
- Why: The stagger recipe is for a list or grid the user sees occasionally, not one they scroll past all day; entrance animations are for content the user asked for and is waiting on.
- Sources: S-L19-017, S-L19-015, S-L19-024

### STD-when-to-animate-14: Tab switches never slide
**must** · react-native, ios, android. Switch between tabs with no animation: set animation: 'none' on Expo Router tabs (NativeTabs keeps the platform's own tab behavior), and never slide, shift or fade between tabs.
- Values: tabs-animation: 'none'
- Why: Tabs are peers, not a hierarchy: sliding implies depth that isn't there, and the user pays for it dozens of times a session.
- `engine.py review` checks it: Tabs are peers switched dozens of times a session: set animation: 'none' instead of shifting or fading between them.
- Sources: S-L19-016, S-L19-015

### STD-when-to-animate-15: Say no when the gate fails
**must**. When a requested animation fails the gate, say so plainly, write no animation code, and offer a non-motion alternative such as an instant state change or a static affordance.
- Why: Animating something that shouldn't animate is the worse failure mode; the gate exists to produce zero lines of code sometimes, and sometimes the best animation is no animation.
- Sources: S-L19-018, S-L19-016, S-L19-012

### STD-when-to-animate-16: Default to restraint when suggesting motion
**must**. When looking for places to add motion, expect to reject most candidates: suggest at most 5-7 for a whole app and fewer for one view, list 2-4 missed opportunities separately in an audit, and say plainly when nothing survives.
- Values: max-suggestions-whole-app: 5-7; missed-opportunities-per-audit: 2-4
- Why: An opportunity finder that suggests motion everywhere produces sluggish, over-animated interfaces; a short list of high-conviction opportunities beats a long wishlist, and if nothing survives the gate that is a good result.
- Sources: S-L19-024, S-L19-027, S-L19-025, S-L19-014

### STD-when-to-animate-17: Delete high-frequency motion first
**must**. Treat animation on a keyboard-initiated or high-frequency action as a blocking, HIGH-severity finding, and fix it (and any animation with no purpose) by deleting the animation before trying any tuning.
- Why: The remedial hierarchy starts with deleting the animation (high-frequency, no purpose, keyboard-triggered); such motion is feel-breaking, and when unsure whether motion feels right the strongest move is often to delete it.
- Sources: S-L19-032, S-L19-027, S-L19-025

### STD-when-to-animate-20: Goal-driven tools need no friction, not delight
**should**. For tools people open with a clear goal (launchers, command menus, everyday work tools), remove unnecessary friction instead of adding delight motion.
- Why: A person opening such a tool has a clear goal, does not expect or need to be delighted, and just wants to work with no unnecessary friction.
- Sources: S-L19-012

### STD-when-to-animate-22: Judge an idea before building it
**should**. Decide deliberately whether an idea deserves to be built before building it, even when AI makes building cheap; building options A and B to compare them is good validation, but only if you actually validate the idea instead of shipping both because it costs little.
- Why: Friction used to force a decision about what was worth making; without it, vibe-coded apps and UI libraries rarely have a thought behind them and feel meaningless. Building A and B is often better validation than theorizing, but only if you actually validate the idea.
- Sources: S-L19-009
